questions.question: Which Python type most directly models a mathematical set?
questions.explanation: Python's set has no order and no duplicates — exactly membership-only structure.

questions.question: You need "everyone who is in admins AND in contractors". In set language that is…
questions.explanation: "Both" is intersection; union is "either", difference is "in one but not the other".

questions.question: Are {1, 2} and {2, 1, 1} the same set?
options: No, because one has a duplicate
Yes — sets have no order and no repeats
questions.explanation: A set is fully determined by what belongs to it; order and repetition simply do not exist.

questions.question: The expression A ⊆ B is a claim that…
options: is true exactly when every member of A is also a member of B
means A is strictly smaller than B
questions.explanation: Operations like ∪ produce sets; ⊆, ∈, = produce truth values. Keeping them straight is half of set fluency.

questions.question: "Users who are not admins" is ambiguous in code unless you also fix…
options: the universe the complement is taken over
questions.explanation: Complement is always relative to a universe — all users, all accounts, all visitors? The lesson's trap example turns on this.

questions.question: De Morgan's law for sets says Ā ∪ B̄ complement equals…
options: Ā ∩ B̄ — complement of union is intersection of complements
questions.explanation: "Not (in A or in B)" is exactly "not in A and not in B" — the set twin of the logic law from the next lesson.

questions.question: The standard proof technique for showing two sets A and B are equal is…
options: double inclusion: A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A
questions.explanation: Each inclusion direction rules out half the possible mismatches; together they force equality for every element.

questions.question: The symmetric difference A △ B contains exactly…
options: elements in both A and B
elements in exactly one of A and B
all elements of A plus all of B
questions.explanation: It is (A − B) ∪ (B − A) — the XOR of sets, verified computationally in the lesson script.

questions.question: Why does brute-forcing a set law over a 4-element universe provide only evidence, not proof?
options: Four elements are too few to compute with
The law must hold over every universe of every size, and finite checks cover only one
questions.explanation: The prose proof by double inclusion works for any universe; the computer check explored one small instance of it.

questions.question: In the proof of ¬(x ∈ A ∪ B) ⇒ x ∈ Ā, the key step is…
options: dividing by the size of A
if x were in A, then x would be in A ∪ B — a contradiction
questions.explanation: Contradiction against the definition of union — the same move used throughout later proofs.

questions.question: SQL's INTERSECT, UNION, and EXCEPT correspond to which set operations?
questions.explanation: Query engines implement exactly the operations defined by membership conditions in this lesson.
